## Definition

The **$p$-th variation** of a [[stochastic-processes|stochastic process]]
measures the accumulated size of its increments raised to the power $p$ along
finer and finer partitions of time.

:::{.definition data-title="$p$-Variation"}

Let $(X_{t})$ be a real-valued continuous-time process and $p>0$. For $t>0$
consider partitions
$$
\Delta^{(n)}:=\{  0 = t_{0}^{(n)}<t_{1}^{(n)}<\dots<t_{K_{n}}^{(n)}=t \}
$$
of $[0,t]$ with mesh
$$
\delta^{(n)}:=\max_{1\leq i\leq K_{n}}\lvert t_{i}^{(n)}-t_{i-1}^{(n)} \rvert \to 0\quad \text{as}\quad n \to \infty.
$$
The **$p$-variation** $\left\langle X,X \right\rangle_{t}^{(p)}$ is the process
(if it exists, and does not depend on the choice of partitions) such that
$$
S_{n}^\Delta = \sum_{i=1}^{K_{n}} \lvert X_{t_{i}^{(n)}}-X_{t_{i-1}^{(n)}} \rvert ^p \stackrel{L_{2}~\&~\mathbb{P}}\to \left\langle X,X \right\rangle_{t}^{(p)}.
$$

:::

In particular:

- for $p=1$ it is the **total variation**; and
- for $p=2$ it is the **quadratic variation**, often written
  $\left< X,X \right>_{t}$.

Quadratic variation is the relevant notion in the $L_{2}$ setting and is key
to the construction of the [[ito-integral]] in [[stochastic-calculus]]. A
smooth (differentiable) path has finite total variation and zero quadratic
variation, since $\sum_i|\Delta X_i|^2\leq\max_i|\Delta X_i|\sum_i|\Delta X_i|\to0$.

## $p$-Variation of Brownian Motion

:::{.theorem data-title="Quadratic Variation of BM"}

For [[brownian-motion]] $\left< B,B \right>_{t}=t$. That is, for partitions
$\Delta^{(n)}$ of $[a,b]$ with $\delta^{(n)}\to 0$,
$S_{n}^\Delta \stackrel{L_{2}~\&~\mathbb{P}}\to b-a$.

:::

:::{.proof}

Write $\Delta_i=t_{i}^{(n)}-t_{i-1}^{(n)}$ and
$\xi_i=B_{t_{i}^{(n)}}-B_{t_{i-1}^{(n)}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Delta_i)$, which are
independent. Then
$\mathbb{E}S_n^\Delta=\sum_i\mathbb{E}\xi_i^2=\sum_i\Delta_i=b-a$ and, using
$\mathbb{E}\xi_i^4=3\Delta_i^2$,
$$
\operatorname{Var}(S_n^\Delta)=\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(\xi_i^2)=\sum_i(3\Delta_i^2-\Delta_i^2)=2\sum_i\Delta_i^2\leq2\delta^{(n)}(b-a)\to0.
$$
Hence $\mathbb{E}|S_n^\Delta-(b-a)|^2=\operatorname{Var}(S_n^\Delta)\to0$, which
is convergence in $L_2$, and so in probability (see
[[convergence-in-lp-norm]]).

:::

:::{.proposition data-title="Brownian Paths Have Infinite Total Variation"}

Almost surely, Brownian motion has infinite total variation on every interval
$[a,b]$ with $a<b$, and hence is not differentiable there.

:::

:::{.proof}

Pass to a subsequence of partitions along which
$S_n^\Delta\to b-a>0$ almost surely. Since Brownian paths are continuous,
hence uniformly continuous on $[a,b]$, $\max_i|\xi_i|\to0$. Then
$$
S_n^\Delta=\sum_i\xi_i^2\leq\max_i|\xi_i|\sum_i|\xi_i|,
$$
so $\sum_i|\xi_i|\geq S_n^\Delta/\max_i|\xi_i|\to\infty$.

:::

Heuristically, with $T=n\Delta t$, $\sum_i|\Delta B_i|\sim n\,\mathbb{E}|B_{\Delta t}|\sim\frac{T}{\Delta t}\sqrt{\Delta t}\to\infty$.
